Check a sweep's inputs before fitting

Source: R/diagnose.R
diagnose_sweep.Rd

Runs the checks a sweep would run, without calling mrds::ddf(), and prints a report of problems found. Use it before sweep_models() to catch a misconfiguration in seconds, instead of after a sweep that errors inside mrds or returns a table that looks valid but is not.

Usage

diagnose_sweep(data, models = NULL, truncation, left = NULL, breaks = NULL)

Arguments

data

Data frame, one row per detection, in the form sweep_models() takes.

models

A model_set(), or NULL (default) for the default set.

truncation

Number. Right truncation distance, in the units of the distances. Required, as for a sweep.

left

Number or NULL (default). Left truncation distance.

breaks

Numeric vector or NULL (default). Bin cutpoints for binned data; derived from the bins when NULL.

Value

Invisibly, a list with the results reached before any stop:

structure

The detection_structure() result, or NULL if the data could not be read.

prepared

The prepare_distance_data() result, or NULL if it failed. Absent if the report stopped earlier.

models

The model set checked. Absent if the report stopped earlier.

The report itself is printed to the console.

Details

The function only reports. It never changes the data or the model set.

How it works

Each finding is printed as one line marked ok, note, WARN or FAIL. A note is a fact about how the survey was flown (for example, a single observer team); it does not count as a problem. WARN and FAIL lines count as problems. A failure marked "stops" below ends the report early.

  1. Refuse to run if truncation is missing (an error, not a report line).

  2. Toolchain: check mrds is installed (WARN if not).

  3. Data: read the table with detection_structure().

    • FAIL and stop if it cannot be read.

    • FAIL if it has no distances; otherwise report the count and type.

    • WARN for each pair of columns that name the same variable.

    • WARN for each analysis whose structure is incomplete (supported is NA), such as a partial double-observer setup.

    • note if perception bias cannot be estimated or there is no size column.

  4. Truncation: run prepare_distance_data().

    • Its warnings are printed as WARN lines. Its errors are printed as a FAIL line and stop the report.

    • Report how many rows were kept, and how many were dropped for each reason.

    • WARN if truncation removes more than 50% of the rows that have a distance.

  5. Sample size: FAIL below 40 detections after truncation, WARN below 60, ok otherwise (Buckland et al. 2001).

  6. Model set: build the default model_set() or check the one given. FAIL and stop if that errors; otherwise list the candidates.

  7. Blind spot: see the section below.

  8. Covariates: FAIL if a formula names a column not in data. Otherwise WARN for a covariate with only one value, and for one with missing values (mrds drops those rows).

  9. Print a reminder that g(0) = 1 is assumed unless corrected at the abundance step. g(0) is the detection probability on the trackline. An error in it scales every candidate equally, so no check here can detect it. See g0().

  10. Print a final line: no problems found, or problems above.

The constant and missing-value covariate checks use the rows that will be fitted, after truncation, since mrds never sees the rest.

Blind-spot check

A blind spot is a strip next to the trackline where the platform cannot see, such as beneath an aircraft. It shows as no detections close to the line.

The check fires when the nearest detection in the input data is more than 2% of truncation from the line. Every dataset has a smallest distance, so a nonzero nearest distance alone is not evidence of a blind spot. The 2% threshold is a heuristic.

There are two treatments, and they are alternatives: left truncation (left), or the gamma key, which models detection rising from zero at the line. The check reports:

SituationResult
Gamma key in the set and left set (blind spot or not)WARN: the blind spot is counted twice.
Blind spot, left set, no gamma keyok
Blind spot, abrupt onsetWARN: a hard edge, which left removes and no key function fits, gamma included.
Blind spot, gradual onset, gamma key in setok
Blind spot, too few detections (under 40) to classify the onset, gamma key in setnote
Blind spot, neither left nor gammaWARN

Abrupt onset means detections start at close to their peak rate just beyond the empty strip. The range from the nearest detection to truncation is cut into 20 equal bins. The onset is abrupt when the first bin's count is more than 60% of the largest bin's count. A geometric edge (a window frame, a hull) gives this shape. A gradual decline in detectability toward the line instead gives a rising first few bins, which is what the gamma key fits. The test needs at least 40 detections; with fewer, the onset is not classed as abrupt.

References

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P., Laake, J.L., Borchers, D.L. and Thomas, L. (2001) Introduction to Distance Sampling. Oxford University Press. Source of the 40 and 60-80 detection guidelines and of trimming roughly the outer 5% of distances.

See also

detection_structure(), which reports what the data could support in principle. sweep_models(), which this is meant to run before.

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(
  object = 1:300,
  distance = c(abs(rnorm(295, 0, 800)), rep(NA, 5)),
  beaufort = sample(0:4, 300, replace = TRUE)
)
diagnose_sweep(d, model_set(c("hn", "hr")), truncation = 2000)
#> dsfit sweep diagnosis
#> 
#> == Toolchain ==
#>   ok    mrds 3.0.1 is installed
#> 
#> == Data ==
#>   ok    300 rows, 295 exact distances
#>   note  estimate perception bias: no double-observer structure: no `observer` or `detected` column
#>   note  carry group size to abundance: no `size` column; abundance would count groups, not individuals
#> 
#> == Truncation ==
#>   ok    293 of 300 rows kept at truncation 2000
#>         dropped: 5 with no distance, 2 beyond the truncation
#>   ok    293 detections is at or above the 60-80 usually suggested
#> 
#> == Model set ==
#>   ok    2 candidates: hn, hr
#> 
#> == What is still assumed ==
#>   g(0) = 1, unless a correction is applied at the abundance step.
#>   Nothing here can detect a wrong one: it scales every candidate
#>   equally, so the ranking looks untouched. See ?g0.
#> 
#> No problems found. Nothing was fitted.
